pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Local weather patterns

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Year 1, Seasonal changes / Working scientifically):** pupils "observe and describe weather associated with the seasons," and might work scientifically by "making tables and charts about the weather."

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-ESS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1].

- **Operational details:** The learning here is PROCEDURAL — children gather their own weather observations and look for patterns, rather than being told facts. Set up a simple, repeated daily routine: each day, observe and record the weather with picture symbols (sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy) and simple measures a 5-year-old can take (is it warm or cold? did it rain?). Keep records on a class chart or pictograph over days and weeks, then read the chart together to describe patterns — 'we had more rainy days than sunny days this week', 'it is colder in the mornings'. The key skills are consistent observation, recording with agreed symbols, and describing (not explaining) what the collected data shows over time. This builds directly on knowing the four seasons and feeds later graph-based seasonal-weather work.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational-procedural, KS1). The child records daily weather with symbols over time and describes simple patterns from the class chart, without needing numerical measurement or causal explanation.
bestPractices: Make it a repeated daily routine so a pattern emerges from many observations over time, not a one-off.
Use agreed picture symbols (sun, cloud, rain, wind, snow) so young children can record consistently without writing.
Keep records visible on a class chart/pictograph and regularly READ it together to describe patterns.
Keep the goal descriptive — what the data shows — not explanatory (no causes of weather yet).
Link the weather record back to the current season so observation and seasonal knowledge reinforce each other.
keyRepresentations: A daily weather chart / calendar filled with picture symbols.
A weekly pictograph or bar of weather types (count of sunny vs rainy days).
Standard weather symbols (sun, cloud, rain, wind, snow).
A warm/cold marker or simple temperature cue.
A 'read the chart' prompt comparing column heights.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a single day's weather represents the whole season or that 'today = always'.
Confusing weather (what it's doing now) with season, or expecting weather to be identical every day.
Reading a pictograph by counting the wrong thing (e.g. the shortest column) or ignoring that each symbol stands for one day.
Believing weather is fully predictable, or conversely totally random with no patterns.
Recording what they wish the weather was rather than what they observe.

learn.summary: For 5–6 year-olds learning local weather patterns, the core skill is procedural: children gather their own daily weather observations with agreed picture symbols, record them over days and weeks on a visible chart or pictograph, then READ the accumulated record together to describe simple patterns (e.g. 'more rainy days than sunny days this week') and make a simple, tentative prediction grounded in that record. The goal is descriptive, not explanatory — no causes of weather yet. The main activity is an ongoing record-and-read routine; vocabulary priming and reading a pre-made pictograph are useful scaffolds with stated limits.

activities.title: Daily weather station: record over time, then read your own chart
feedback: If the chart has gaps or the categories change day to day, prompt: use the same simple symbols, recorded at the same time each day, so a pattern can appear.
When reading, ask simple pattern questions aloud ('which column is tallest?' 'more rainy or sunny days?') and let the child answer by comparing column heights.
If a child records what they wish the weather was instead of what they see, ask them to look outside again and record what is actually happening now.
If a child predicts tomorrow from a wish ('sunny because I want to play out'), ask what the weather has actually been doing and what is likely next based on the recorded pattern.
If a child expects the weather to be identical every day within a season, note that days still differ within a season — that is exactly why we record over time and look for patterns.
Remind that each symbol stands for one day, so the taller column shows the weather that happened on more days; if unsure, count the day-symbols within each column together.
For pre-readers, read prompts and symbol names aloud so the reading step does not depend on text.
For safety, point children to shadows on the ground and the general daylight to tell it is sunny, and remind them never to look straight at the sun.
activities.rationale: The standard is a repeated observe–record–read-the-pattern procedure that also feeds a simple prediction, so the activity should enact it: logging each day, watching a pictograph build, reading the accumulated pattern, and predicting tentatively from it. A physical class weather chart is the essential hands-on form; a screen weather-station may model the same routine and let children replay a whole week quickly, but it complements rather than replaces the real daily observation.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils observe and describe weather associated with the seasons and may make tables and charts about the weather.
learnerActions: Each day, look outside and choose today's weather symbol(s) from an agreed set: sun, cloud, rain, wind, snow. To tell if it is sunny, look at shadows on the ground (sharp shadows mean sunshine) and the overall daylight — never look directly at the sun.
Add a simple warm/cold marker (is it warm or cold today?).
Place that day's entry onto a growing weekly chart or pictograph so a column builds up for each weather type.
At the end of the week, step back and READ the chart: which column is tallest? Say the pattern aloud — e.g. 'this week was more rainy than sunny.'

Use the pattern to make a simple prediction about tomorrow, and say what on the chart makes you think so (e.g. 'it's been rainy most days, so maybe rainy again') — keeping it a guess, not a certainty.
Keep the routine going into a new week and compare: did the pattern change?
Link the record to the current season so weather observation and seasonal knowledge reinforce each other.
activities.intendedInsight: A pattern emerges from many observations collected over time; children can describe what their own data shows, and base a simple prediction on it, rather than being told a fact.

activities.title: Weather-symbol vocabulary primer
feedback: If a symbol is mismatched, replay the name and point to the matching picture.
Encourage saying the weather word aloud while pointing to the symbol.
activities.rationale: Agreed picture symbols let young children record without writing. A vocabulary primer builds this shared code first; it is a preparatory scaffold that teaches the names, but on its own it does not elicit the record-over-time-and-find-a-pattern skill that is the heart of the standard.
learnerActions: Explore an illustrated sky scene and tap or point to each weather type.
Hear and say its name (sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy) and see its matching symbol.
Match each weather symbol to its spoken name before starting the weather diary.
activities.intendedInsight: Children learn the shared vocabulary and symbols for weather types so they can record consistently later.

activities.title: Read a finished weather pictograph
feedback: If the child picks the shortest column, remind them 'most days' means the taller column.
If they ignore that each symbol is one day, count the symbols in a column together.
If the child reads the wrong column, point at and compare the two columns side by side.
activities.rationale: Reading a pre-made pictograph is a checkable sub-skill and a useful support, but a fixed set of questions on a finished chart does not include the ongoing daily recording that defines the skill. Use it to practise chart-reading, not as a substitute for collecting data over time.
learnerActions: Look at a simple pre-made weather pictograph of a week.
Answer aloud: which column is tallest? Were there more rainy or sunny days?
Match weather symbols to their names.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a completed pictograph means checking what each symbol stands for (in this chart, one symbol = one day), then comparing column heights, which works when the symbols are the same size and evenly spaced, or counting the symbols in each column.

constraints: Keep the goal descriptive — what the data shows — not explanatory; causes of weather are not introduced at this age.
The real daily classroom weather chart with genuine outdoor observation is essential; a screen weather-station may model the routine but does not replace observing the actual weather each day.
A vocabulary poster teaches weather-word names only; it does not enact recording over time or finding a pattern.
Reading a pre-made pictograph practises chart-reading but omits the ongoing daily recording that defines the procedural skill — use it as a scaffold, not the main activity.
Record what is actually observed, not what the child wishes the weather to be, and base predictions on the record rather than a wish, keeping predictions tentative.
For safety, children should judge sunshine from shadows on the ground and general daylight and must never look directly at the sun.
Numerical measurement and causal explanation are not required at this checkpoint (concrete/observational-procedural, KS1).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row asserted '3D adds nothing' and that 'dialogue cannot substitute' — these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. They have been reframed: spatial/3D framing is simply not needed for a charting task, and open dialogue demands language beyond age 5 as a practical limit, not an absolute impossibility.
The NGSS K-ESS2-1 source is marked verified:false in the row; the UK DfE source is marked verified:true. Evidence strength is not upgraded here.

The row's description mentions 'recording temperature, rainfall' numerically, while the checkpoint states no numerical measurement is needed at this age; activities use warm/cold and simple categories consistent with the checkpoint, treating precise measurement as beyond this tier.
Simple prediction is retained because it is required by the objective and assessment, but is framed as a tentative guess from the recent record rather than a reliable forecast.

probeDeeper: Looking at your chart, what has the weather been like most days this week?
What do you think tomorrow will be like, and what on your chart makes you think so?
Why do we write it down each day instead of just remembering?
assess.correctAnswer: Records each day's conditions consistently with clear symbols or words, keeps it going over time, spots a simple pattern (e.g. 'it's been rainy all week,' 'colder in the mornings') and makes a sensible prediction grounded in the recent record.

errorPatterns.pattern: Records inconsistently or only once, so no pattern can appear
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the same simple categories, recorded at the same time each day.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gaps in the chart; categories change day to day

errorPatterns.pattern: Predicts from a wish, not the record ('sunny because I want to play out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask: 'what has the weather been doing, and what is likely next?'

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The weather is the same every day in a season' — doesn't expect day-to-day variation
errorPatterns.nextMove: Within a season days still differ — that's why we record and look for patterns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: assumes the season fixes each day exactly, so recording seems pointless

responseLevels.gap: Can't record consistently; has no usable chart; prediction unrelated to observations.
responseLevels.full: Observes and records systematically over time, identifies a simple pattern from the record, and makes a sensible prediction grounded in it — and could keep the routine going.
responseLevels.partial: Records daily but inconsistently, or reads the chart but predicts without using the pattern.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Over a week or two, ask the child to observe the weather each day and record it on a simple chart (sunny/cloudy/rainy, warm/cold, windy). Then ask them to point out any pattern and predict tomorrow. Watch how they observe, record consistently, and read their own chart — don't ask them to define 'weather.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching reveals whether the child observes and records systematically day to day and reads their own data, versus recording once, inconsistently, or predicting from a wish rather than the chart.

sources.claim: Year 1 pupils observe and describe weather associated with the seasons and may make tables and charts about the weather.
